items.title: Within Our Power
items.question: In the Stoic dichotomy of control, what is the one thing fully within our power?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The Stoics locate freedom in what the mind does with events rather than in the events themselves.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is our judgements. Outcomes depend on countless factors, but the verdict we place on them is ours to shape.
items.lessonContent:
Separate what you influence from what you do not.
Attention spent on externals is often wasted.
Your response is the part you author.
Practise sorting decisions into the two columns.
Share this: sort tonight one worry into what you control and what you do not.

items.title: Beyond Our Power
items.question: According to Epictetus, which category includes reputation, wealth, and the actions of other people?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. These are the externals, which can be influenced but never guaranteed by us.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is external events. Treating them as fully ours sets us up for frustration, because their outcome is not in our hands.
items.lessonContent:
Some goods are never guaranteed.
Wanting only what is certain avoids disappointment.
Influence is not the same as control.
Accept the gap between effort and outcome.
Share this: name tonight one outcome you must release.

items.title: Opinions Disturb
items.question: Epictetus taught that people are disturbed not by events but by what?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The disturbance comes from the interpretation, not the bare fact.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is their opinions. Change the interpretation and the emotional charge changes with it.
items.lessonContent:
Emotion follows appraisal, not events.
Interpretations can be examined and revised.
Pause between stimulus and reaction.
Test whether a judgement is accurate.
Share this: catch tonight one event you have loaded with an opinion.

items.title: Imagining Loss
items.question: What is the Stoic practice of imagining the loss of what you value, in order to appreciate it more?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Briefly rehearsing loss restores gratitude for what is already present.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is negative visualisation. The exercise is not morbid but a way to see present goods clearly.
items.lessonContent:
Contrast sharpens appreciation.
Imagined loss reveals hidden value.
Familiarity dulls gratitude.
Use the exercise briefly, not habitually.
Share this: imagine losing one comfort tonight, then notice it again.

items.title: Ruler and Writer
items.question: Marcus Aurelius wrote his private philosophical notes while leading which state?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The emperor wrote the Meditations for himself amid the pressures of ruling.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the Roman Empire. The notes were a personal discipline, never intended for publication.
items.lessonContent:
Philosophy can be practised amid power.
Private notes often hold the most honest thinking.
Writing is a form of self-discipline.
Even rulers must manage their own minds.
Share this: write tonight one line of guidance to yourself.

items.title: Turn It Around
items.question: In Stoic practice, what can an obstacle in your path become if you use it well?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The impediment can be redirected into material for action and growth.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is an opportunity. The obstacle itself is neutral; what we make of it is the variable.
items.lessonContent:
Blockages can be reframed as material.
Action is often the cure for frustration.
Difficulty trains capacities that ease cannot.
Ask what the obstacle makes possible.
Share this: reframe tonight one obstacle as a prompt to act.

items.title: Inner Victory
items.question: Which conquest did the Stoics consider more important than any military victory?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Self-mastery was the harder and more valuable victory.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the self. External triumphs are fleeting, while governing your own impulses shapes everything.
items.lessonContent:
Inner discipline outlasts outer wins.
Self-command is a trainable skill.
Mastery begins with attention to impulse.
Measure progress by conduct, not trophies.
Share this: choose tonight one impulse to hold back for an hour.

items.title: Remember Mortality
items.question: What Latin phrase names the Stoic practice of remembering that you will die?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The reminder of mortality was meant to sharpen, not sadden, how one lives.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is memento mori. Facing finitude clarifies what deserves your limited time.
items.lessonContent:
Finitude gives urgency to choices.
Awareness of death can clarify priorities.
Use mortality as a lens, not a weight.
Spend time as the scarce resource it is.
Share this: ask tonight what you would do if time were short.

items.title: Flourishing Life
items.question: What Greek term do the Stoics use for the flourishing life that virtue aims at?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Eudaimonia describes a life well lived rather than a passing feeling of pleasure.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is eudaimonia. It names a sustained condition of living well, not a momentary mood.
items.lessonContent:
Well-being is a life, not a moment.
Virtue is both the path and the goal.
Distinguish pleasure from flourishing.
Judge success by the whole, not one day.
Share this: define tonight one marker of a life going well for you.

items.title: Some Things Up To Us
items.question: Which Stoic teacher opened his handbook by dividing things into those up to us and those not up to us?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The former slave began the Enchiridion with that famous division.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is Epictetus. His handbook opens by sorting everything into the controllable and the uncontrollable.
items.lessonContent:
A simple distinction can reorganise a life.
Teachers shape how a school is remembered.
Start with first principles.
Return to the basic division when confused.
Share this: apply one foundational distinction to today's decisions.

items.title: Imagined Troubles
items.question: Seneca said we suffer more in which realm than in reality?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Anticipated misfortunes often cause more distress than the events themselves.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is imagination. Most feared scenarios never arrive, yet they are lived through in advance.
items.lessonContent:
Fear projects suffering ahead of events.
Imagined pain is paid before it is due.
Distinguish a real problem from a rehearsed one.
Return to what is actually present.
Share this: notice tonight one trouble you have suffered only in advance.

items.title: Inner Fortress
items.question: The Stoics described an untouchable refuge a person can always retreat to. What is it?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The mind was seen as a fortress no external force can breach without consent.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the mind. Circumstances can constrain the body but need not occupy the inner life.
items.lessonContent:
An inner refuge is always available.
External force cannot command your assent.
Withdraw there to recover perspective.
Protect it by guarding what you admit.
Share this: pause tonight in a quiet mental retreat for one minute.

items.title: Calm Under Pressure
items.question: What name do the Stoics give to the steady calm that survives misfortune?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Equanimity is the evenness of mind that neither swells nor collapses with events.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is equanimity. It is not indifference but a stable footing from which to respond.
items.lessonContent:
Calm is a trained state, not a temperament.
Evenness allows clearer action.
Distinguish calm from apathy.
Build it through small daily practice.
Share this: practise one even response to a minor irritation today.

items.title: Rehearsing Loss
items.question: The Latin phrase premeditatio malorum describes rehearsing what kind of thing in advance?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Deliberately imagining possible difficulties reduces their shock and prepares a response.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is future troubles. The rehearsal is meant to build readiness, not anxiety.
items.lessonContent:
Preparation reduces the force of surprise.
Rehearsing difficulty builds steadiness.
Do it briefly and constructively.
Pair every imagined problem with a response.
Share this: rehearse tonight one difficulty and plan your answer to it.

items.title: Gymnasium of Hardship
items.question: What does a Stoic turn a difficulty into when it cannot be avoided?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Hard circumstances become a gymnasium for the virtues, if approached that way.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is training. The same event that crushes one person can strengthen another who treats it as practice.
items.lessonContent:
Hardship can be repurposed as practice.
Attitude determines whether it builds or breaks.
Seek the lesson inside the difficulty.
Progress shows in how you meet repeats.
Share this: treat tonight one annoyance as deliberate practice.

items.title: Private Notebook
items.question: Marcus Aurelius wrote the Meditations primarily for whom?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The book is a private notebook of reminders, never aimed at readers.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is himself. Knowing it was private explains its repeated, blunt self-exhortations.
items.lessonContent:
Private writing encourages honesty.
Reminders work best when repeated.
Write to think, not to impress.
Revisit your own notes over time.
Share this: write tonight one reminder you need to hear again.

items.title: Labels We Add
items.question: If events are neither good nor bad in themselves, what makes them appear so to us?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. We add the label of good or bad, and then respond to our own label.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is assessments. Recognising the added label is the first step to revising it.
items.lessonContent:
Value is often assigned, not discovered.
Notice the moment you label an event.
Labels can be tested for accuracy.
Freedom grows as labels loosen.
Share this: catch tonight one automatic good-or-bad label you apply.

items.title: Guard Attention
items.question: What do the Stoics say you should do with your attention and assent?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Attention and assent are the gates through which impressions become beliefs.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is guard it. Careless assent lets stray impressions harden into convictions.
items.lessonContent:
Beliefs form from impressions you admit.
Pause before agreeing with a thought.
Attention is a limited resource.
Defend it from noise and manipulation.
Share this: pause tonight before accepting one strong impression.

items.title: Chosen Hardship
items.question: What is the Stoic exercise of choosing mild hardship on purpose, to build resilience?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Deliberately forgoing comfort teaches that it is not required for contentment.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is voluntary discomfort. The point is to reduce dependence on ease, not to seek suffering.
items.lessonContent:
Testing discomfort builds tolerance.
Wanting less increases freedom.
Choose mild challenges, not self-punishment.
Notice that comfort is optional.
Share this: deliberately skip one small comfort today.

items.title: View From Above
items.question: The Stoic exercise of imagining your life from a great height is meant to give what?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Zooming out restores proportion and shrinks the apparent size of troubles.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is perspective. Seeing your concerns against the whole reduces their grip without dismissing them.
items.lessonContent:
Scale changes the feeling of a problem.
Zoom out to restore proportion.
Context reduces the power of a moment.
Return to your own size deliberately.
Share this: imagine tonight your day from far above, then continue it.

items.title: Only True Good
items.question: For the Stoics, what alone is genuinely good, independent of circumstance?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Virtue is the only unconditional good, since it cannot be taken away by fortune.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is virtue. Health, wealth, and reputation are preferred but not necessary for living well.
items.lessonContent:
Distinguish unconditional goods from preferred ones.
Fortune cannot remove good character.
Rank values by dependability.
Invest in what cannot be confiscated.
Share this: name tonight one good no one can take from you.

items.title: Only True Evil
items.question: The Stoics held that only one condition corrupts a person no matter the circumstance. What is it?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Vice, the corruption of character, is the only unconditional evil.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is vice. Pain and loss are unwelcome but not evils in the moral sense the Stoics mean.
items.lessonContent:
Harm to character outweighs harm to comfort.
Rank misfortunes by what they damage.
Guard integrity above advantage.
Judge events by their effect on character.
Share this: weigh tonight one choice by its effect on your character.

items.title: Only Now
items.question: What do the Stoics advise regarding the past and the future?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Since only the present can be acted on, the Stoics place attention there.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is live in the present. Brooding on the past or dreading the future spends energy on what cannot be touched.
items.lessonContent:
Only this moment can be acted on.
Regret and dread both spend the present.
Attend to the task at hand.
Plan, then return to now.
Share this: bring your attention back to the present once tonight.

items.title: Cosmic Reason
items.question: What do the Stoics call the rational order that pervades the universe?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The logos is the rational principle the Stoics saw running through nature and mind alike.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the logos. Living in agreement with it meant aligning conduct with reason and nature.
items.lessonContent:
Ancient thinkers sought order in the cosmos.
Aligning with nature was an ethical aim.
Reason linked the human and the universal.
Borrow ideas without adopting the whole system.
Share this: consider tonight how one choice fits a larger order.

items.title: Evening Review
items.question: What did many Stoics do at the end of the day to examine their conduct?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. A nightly review traced the day's actions and identified what to improve.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is an evening review. Looking back calmly converts experience into improvement.
items.lessonContent:
Reflection turns experience into learning.
Review without harsh self-judgement.
Name one thing to do differently tomorrow.
Keep the ritual brief and regular.
Share this: review tonight one action and name one change for tomorrow.
